title: Retrieving Better: A Guide to Retrieval Practice https://www.carousel-learning.com/teaching-and-learning/resources/tag/Retrieving-Better
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 17, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises Adam Boxer's practitioner guide Retrieving Better, which sets out both the theory and the practical rollout of retrieval practice in schools. The guide argues retrieval practice reliably enhances long-term learning and lays out methods — questioning based on prior learning, self-quizzing, and structured homework — for putting it into effect. Boxer stresses that feedback timing matters: immediate, directive feedback works best early in learning, while delayed, less specific feedback suits more expert learners. A large section addresses homework design through four levers — access, purposeful thinking, accountability, and value — and introduces the distinction between Completion Ratio and Think Ratio as ways to judge whether homework is actually promoting deep engagement. Barton also draws out Boxer's guidance on using technology and Whole Class Feedback to reduce teacher workload while keeping retrieval practice visible and valued to students.
points: Distinguishing Completion Ratio (how many students finish homework) from Think Ratio (how much deep thinking it provokes) gives teachers a sharper lens for evaluating retrieval homework.
Feedback should shift from immediate and directive early in learning to delayed and less specific as students gain expertise.
Homework design should be judged against four levers: access, purposeful thinking, accountability, and value — not simply whether it was completed.
Whole Class Feedback is positioned as a tool for surfacing common misconceptions from retrieval homework and turning them into targeted class discussion.
Technology should be used to reduce, not add to, teacher workload — via activity reduction, efficiency gains, and easier collaboration.
quotes: Retrieval practice is a highly effective strategy for enhancing long-term student learning.
It is crucial to provide students with feedback on their retrieval practice, especially when they are initially learning new material.
Homework can be an effective tool for extending retrieval practice beyond the classroom.

When assessing the impact of homework, it is essential to distinguish between Completion Ratio (the number of students completing the homework) and Think Ratio (the extent to which the homework promotes deep thinking and learning).
Technology, when used thoughtfully, can effectively reduce teacher workload.
Whole Class Feedback (WCF) is a valuable tool for identifying common misconceptions and facilitating class discussions.
Does retrieval practice improve student learning in school and classroom settings? Based on our literature review, our response for researchers and educators is an unequivocal yes.
